docs.text: nixos-homelab-finance Personal finance apps on top of nixos-homelab : budgeting and portfolio tracking, plus companion services that keep them in sync with each other and with external data sources. For the full list of module options, see the options reference . docs.text: nixos-homelab-networking The networking base that ties the rest of the homelab together. Every workload across every nixos-homelab-* repo declares allowIngress / allowEgress on its kubenix workload -- this repo's cilium module is what actually enforces them as network policy; without it they're just labels. It also provides the CNI itself, inbound and outbound VPNs, routable IP pools, and DNS management. See the Cilium network policies docs for the policies this repo's cilium module gives kubenix pods and lib.toPorts , and the options reference for the full list of module options. Setup { inputs = { ... homelab-networking = { url = "github:nixos-homelab/networking"; inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs"; }; ... }; } { inputs, ... }: { imports = [ inputs.homelab-networking.nixosModules.cilium ]; config.homelab.cilium.enable = true; } Modules cilium : the Cilium CNI, plus the LoadBalancer IP pool it hands out from -- see the Cilium network policies docs for the policies it gives the pods of kubenix submodules. routed-ippool : a routable IPv4 pool for LoadBalancer services, routed to the cluster from the LAN. client-vpn : the inbound WireGuard gateway -- named access groups, each scoped to specific services or full cluster access, for remote kubectl /service access. privacy-vpn : an outbound WireGuard tunnel to an external VPN provider, for routing a workload's egress traffic through it (e.g. homelab-media 's rtorrent ). external-dns : external-dns , managing DNS records for cluster services automatically. unifi : Unifi Network Controller, for managing Ubiquiti networking gear. netutils : a debugging container with common networking tools, for troubleshooting from inside the cluster.

docs.text: Cilium network policies The policies of kubenix pods, the Cilium types and lib.toPorts . kubenix pods The policies of the CNI-neutral intent of every instance of a submodule that runs pods, or of pods (the feature pod-policy ), added through kubenix submodules.defaults when homelab.cilium.enable is set. They select the pods by app.kubernetes.io/name of the instance, or the selector of pods : policyPorts , all of ports unless set: pods labeled cluster.local/<name>-egress: allow in any namespace may reach them, through the CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy pod-to-<name> and the CiliumNetworkPolicy <name>-from-pod . apiServerPorts : the API server may reach them, <name>-from-apiserver . worldPorts : the world outside the cluster may reach them, <name>-from-world . They go in the manifest of the instance; change them through its config , as kubernetes.resources.ciliumNetworkPolicies.<name>-from-pod . Cilium types nixosModules.cilium-crds (which cilium imports) adds the kubenix types of the Cilium CRDs, of the version of the chart cilium installs, and hands the CRDs to the manifests check through homelab.cluster.runtimeCRDs , as Cilium's operator creates them at runtime. It deploys nothing: a module that writes Cilium policies by hand imports it, so it evaluates with Cilium off too. lib.toPorts Cilium's toPorts from a flat list of ports as a NetworkPolicy writes them, for policies written by hand: port numbers, or { port; protocol; } (and endPort ). Cilium wants the port as a string. No ports give null, which leaves the field out. homelab.kubernetes.kubernetes.resources.ciliumNetworkPolicies.dns.spec.egress = [ { toEntities = [ "world" ]; toPorts = inputs.homelab-networking.lib.toPorts [ { port = 53; protocol = "UDP"; } 443 ]; } ]; gives toPorts = [ { ports = [ { port = "53"; protocol = "UDP"; } { port = "443"; } ]; } ] .

docs.text: nixos-homelab-shared Every other nixos-homelab-* repo takes this one as an input and builds on its cluster module, the facts of the cluster, with a runner that runs it: the k3s module, enabled. It also provides shared services used across those repos: a dashboard, TLS, and SSH-key access to the cluster. Databases and storage are in nixos-homelab-storage . See the kubenix docs for the typed resources and submodules of homelab.kubernetes , and the options reference for the full list of module options. Setup { inputs = { ... homelab-shared = { url = "github:nixos-homelab/shared"; inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs"; }; ... }; } { inputs, ... }: { imports = [ inputs.homelab-shared.nixosModules.k3s ]; config.homelab.k3s.enable = true; } Modules cluster : the shared homelab.cluster.* options every other module in this ecosystem builds on, whichever runner runs the cluster: IP families, pod/service CIDRs, debug tools, backup aggregation, the images to preload and the manifests to apply, and the facts the runner sets (kubeconfig, unit, Kubernetes version). k3s : runs the cluster on k3s ( homelab.k3s ): it imports cluster , preloads its images, applies its manifests, and drains the node at shutdown. workloads : the settings every workload shares ( homelab.workloads : domain, gateway class, ACME issuer, pod user and group) and kubenix configuration in homelab.kubernetes , with the workload submodule -- see the kubenix docs . cluster imports it and hands what it holds to the runner. homepage : the homepage dashboard, with a per-service integrations allow-list. cert-manager : cert-manager plus a LibDNS ACME webhook, for automated TLS certificates. k8sss : deploys k8sss for SSH-key-based kubectl access.

docs.text: kubenix The workloads module holds the settings every workload shares, in homelab.workloads ( domain , gatewayClassName , acmeProvider , containerUtils , securityContext ), and the submodules below. homelab.kubernetes takes kubenix configuration of the cluster: typed Kubernetes resources, so a misspelled field fails at evaluation and names where it was set. Each submodule instance goes to the runner as a manifest of its own, named after the instance; the other objects go to the manifest kubenix . Custom resources The custom resources are typed too, from the CRDs: lib.crd2types.customTypes turns a CustomResourceDefinition into kubenix customTypes , at evaluation, so a bump of a CRD retypes its resources. This module types Gateway API's experimental channel, as pinned in lib.crds.pinned ; the cert-manager module adds those of its chart, and the module of the CNI its own (networking's cilium-crds ). Every submodule gets them. Their attribute names are kubenix's: the plural cased like the kind ( gateways , hTTPRoutes , ciliumNetworkPolicies , certificates , clusterIssuers ). Optional fields default to null and are left out; value validations (patterns, bounds, CEL rules) stay with the API server. A list the CRD merges by one key takes an attribute set by that key, like the lists kubenix keys in its core types: Gateway listeners by name , so an instance changes one listener of its Gateway ( mkForce where the workload sets the field already): homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.grafana.config.kubernetes.resources.gateways.grafana.spec.listeners.grafana.port = lib.mkForce 8443; A list still works there; its items keep their order, ahead of those given by key. A CRD that starts using a schema construct crd2types doesn't know fails evaluation, naming where. homelab.kubernetes.kubernetes.resources.certificates.plex = { metadata.namespace = "plex"; spec = { secretName = "plex-tls"; dnsNames = [ "plex.example.org" ]; issuerRef = { kind = "ClusterIssuer"; name = "letsencrypt-production"; }; }; }; A module adds the types of a CRD it installs to homelab.kubernetes.kubernetes.customTypes . Cluster-scoped resources need metadata.namespace = null . workload A long-running workload: a Namespace and a Deployment named after the instance, and depending on the args a PersistentVolumeClaim, a Service and a Gateway with its HTTPRoutes. homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.grafana = { submodule = "workload"; args = { allowEgress = [ "internet" "mimir" "postgresql" ]; dataPath = "/var/lib/grafana"; ingressPort = 3000; ports.web = 3000; container = { image = "grafana:latest"; env = [ { name = "GF_PATHS_DATA"; value = "/var/lib/grafana"; } ]; }; }; }; container : the main container, named after the instance, as kubenix's Container type. It's locked down by default ( allowPrivilegeEscalation = false , read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, NET_BIND_SERVICE added when it has ports); set securityContext.capabilities.add for more. ports : the container ports by name, a port number or { containerPort; protocol; } . They also make the Service, with the same names. dataPath : a 1Gi PersistentVolumeClaim named after the workload, mounted here in the main container. ingressPort : a Gateway at <gateway.subdomain>.<gateway.domain> (the bare domain when gateway.subdomain = null ) routing to this Service port, with a redirect from HTTP; allows ingress from gateway . httpRouteRules go ahead of the catch-all rule. policyPorts : the names of the ports other pods may reach, all of them by default; see below. apiServerPorts , worldPorts : the names of the ports the API server and the world outside the cluster may reach, none by default. allowIngress / allowEgress : the pod labels cluster.local/<workload>-ingress / -egress: allow , for the label selectors of the network policies. The workload holds no network policies of its own, only this intent ( policy.nix ). The module of the CNI turns it into policies for every instance with the feature pod-policy through submodules.defaults : networking's cilium lets pods labeled cluster.local/<workload>-egress: allow reach the policyPorts , and so on. Without a CNI module there are none. - securityContext : runAsUser , runAsGroup (also the fsGroup ) and supplementalGroups of the pod. They default to homelab.workloads.securityContext , as gateway.domain , gateway.className and gateway.issuer default to the domain , gatewayClassName and acmeProvider there. Anything else goes on the instance config , where the objects are kubenix resources. Lists kubenix keys by name (containers, volumes, ports) take attribute sets: homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.unifi.config.kubernetes.resources = { services.unifi.spec.type = "LoadBalancer"; deployments.unifi.spec.template.spec.volumes.config.hostPath.path = "/srv/unifi"; }; pod-spec.nix holds the main container and the pod security context for every submodule that runs pods; submodules.defaults with features = [ "pod-spec" ] reaches all of them. deployment, daemonset, job, cronjob, script The pod alone, in the resource that runs it, named after the instance: container , ports , policyPorts , apiServerPorts , worldPorts , allowIngress , allowEgress and securityContext as in the workload, with no Namespace or Service. A Deployment is recreated on change; the pod of a Job or CronJob isn't restarted unless the instance sets restartPolicy . cronjob takes the schedule . script runs a bash script once: a ConfigMap and a Job, the script mounted at a path hashed from it, so a changed script changes the pod template of the Job, the runner replaces the Job and it runs again. It runs in image , the container-utils of the cluster unless set. homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.backup-grafana-db = { submodule = "cronjob"; args = { schedule = "10 3 * * *"; allowEgress = [ "postgresql" ]; container = { image = "postgresql:latest"; command = [ "pg_dump" "--file=/dumps/grafana.pgdump" ]; volumeMounts."/dumps".name = "dumps"; }; }; config.kubernetes.resources.cronJobs.backup-grafana-db.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.volumes.dumps.persistentVolumeClaim.claimName = "database-dumps"; }; service A Service named after the instance, selecting the pods named so. ports by name: a port number, or the fields of a ServicePort. homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.alloy = { submodule = "service"; args.ports.web = 3000; }; pods The policy intent of pods something else runs (a release, a static manifest, another module): ports , policyPorts , apiServerPorts and worldPorts as in the workload, for the pods with the labels selector in the namespace of the instance, app.kubernetes.io/name of the instance name unless set. It writes no objects; the CNI module adds the policies as for any pod. homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.cert-manager.config.submodules.instances.webhook = { name = "cert-manager-webhook"; submodule = "pods"; args = { selector = { "app.kubernetes.io/name" = "webhook"; "app.kubernetes.io/instance" = "cert-manager"; }; ports.https = 10250; apiServerPorts = [ "https" ]; }; }; manifest Objects that go to the runner together: the resources on the instance config and the instances nested in it. Every top-level instance is one manifest, and the runner deletes what a manifest stops holding. An object that moves to another manifest is deleted when the runner applies the old manifest first, and a Namespace or a PersistentVolumeClaim takes what it holds with it. So objects that went to the runner together stay in one manifest , under the old name. homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.cert-manager = { submodule = "manifest"; config = { kubernetes.resources.namespaces.cert-manager.metadata.namespace = null; submodules.instances = { webhook = { name = "cert-manager-webhook-libdns"; submodule = "deployment"; args.container.image = "cert-manager-webhook-libdns:latest"; }; webhook-service = { name = "cert-manager-webhook-libdns"; submodule = "service"; args.ports.https = { port = 443; targetPort = 8443; }; }; }; }; }; All submodules, workload and manifest included, put their objects in the namespace of the instance they're nested in, or the one named after the instance at the top; set config.kubernetes.namespace for another. Two nested instances whose objects share a name, like a Deployment and the Service in front of it, take keys of their own and the object name as name .

docs.text: A long-running workload: a Namespace and a Deployment named after the instance, and depending on the args a PersistentVolumeClaim, a Service and a Gateway with its HTTPRoutes. homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.grafana = { submodule = "workload"; args = { allowEgress = [ "internet" "mimir" "postgresql" ]; dataPath = "/var/lib/grafana"; ingressPort = 3000; ports.web = 3000; container = { image = "grafana:latest"; env = [ { name = "GF_PATHS_DATA"; value = "/var/lib/grafana"; } ]; }; }; }; container : the main container, named after the instance, as kubenix's Container type. It's locked down by default ( allowPrivilegeEscalation = false , read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, NET_BIND_SERVICE added when it has ports); set securityContext.capabilities.add for more. ports : the container ports by name, a port number or { containerPort; protocol; } . They also make the Service, with the same names. dataPath : a 1Gi PersistentVolumeClaim named after the workload, mounted here in the main container. ingressPort : a Gateway at <gateway.subdomain>.<gateway.domain> (the bare domain when gateway.subdomain = null ) routing to this Service port, with a redirect from HTTP; allows ingress from gateway . httpRouteRules go ahead of the catch-all rule. policyPorts : the names of the ports other pods may reach, all of them by default; see below. apiServerPorts , worldPorts : the names of the ports the API server and the world outside the cluster may reach, none by default. allowIngress / allowEgress : the pod labels cluster.local/<workload>-ingress / -egress: allow , for the label selectors of the network policies. The workload holds no network policies of its own, only this intent ( policy.nix ). The module of the CNI turns it into policies for every instance with the feature pod-policy through submodules.defaults : networking's cilium lets pods labeled cluster.local/<workload>-egress: allow reach the policyPorts , and so on. Without a CNI module there are none. - securityContext : runAsUser , runAsGroup (also the fsGroup ) and supplementalGroups of the pod. They default to homelab.workloads.securityContext , as gateway.domain , gateway.className and gateway.issuer default to the domain , gatewayClassName and acmeProvider there. Anything else goes on the instance config , where the objects are kubenix resources. Lists kubenix keys by name (containers, volumes, ports) take attribute sets: homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.unifi.config.kubernetes.resources = { services.unifi.spec.type = "LoadBalancer"; deployments.unifi.spec.template.spec.volumes.config.hostPath.path = "/srv/unifi"; }; pod-spec.nix holds the main container and the pod security context for every submodule that runs pods; submodules.defaults with features = [ "pod-spec" ] reaches all of them.

docs.text: images lib.images.pinned The upstream images pinned in a Dockerfile, as image archives for homelab.cluster.images . Dependabot bumps the FROM name:tag@digest lines; their Nix hashes are in images.lock next to the Dockerfile, which nix run github:nixos-homelab/shared#lock-images updates. The tag gets the digest's first 12 hex digits, so a bump changes the pod spec and rolls the workload. Each archive's ref is its name:tag . Arguments pkgs : nixpkgs dockerfile ( Path ): Dockerfile with one FROM line per image Example let redis = (images.pinned pkgs ./Dockerfile).redis; in { homelab.cluster.images = [ redis ]; # ... image = redis.ref; imagePullPolicy = "Never"; } lib.images.locked Image archives for refs that something upstream names (a chart, another module), locked to a digest and hash in lockFile , which lock-images --lock FILE REF... writes. Returns the archives for homelab.cluster.images and refFor , which maps each ref to its archive's name:tag (the tag suffixed with the digest's first 12 hex digits). Arguments pkgs : nixpkgs lockFile ( Path ): JSON of ref to { digest, hash } refs ( [String] ): image refs, with or without a digest lib.images.chart A rendered manifest (a Helm chart's, say) with every image: ref replaced by its locked archive, see locked . Reading the manifest builds it during evaluation. Returns manifest , images and refs (what the manifest names, for lock-images --lock ). Arguments pkgs : nixpkgs lockFile ( Path ): JSON of ref to { digest, hash } manifest ( Path ): the rendered manifest

docs.text: ipv4 lib.ipv4.ip Build an "ip record" -- { a; b; c; d; prefixLength; address; } , the shape every other function in this library takes and returns -- from four octets and a CIDR prefix length. Arguments a , b , c , d ( Int ): The four octets prefixLength ( Int ): The CIDR prefix length Example ip 10 42 0 5 16 => { a = 10; b = 42; c = 0; d = 5; prefixLength = 16; address = "10.42.0.5"; } lib.ipv4.cidrIndex Offset an ip record by idx addresses, keeping the same prefixLength . Arguments ip : The ip record to offset idx ( Int ): How many addresses to add (or, if negative, subtract) Example toCIDR (cidrIndex (fromString "10.42.0.0/24") 5) => "10.42.0.5/24" lib.ipv4.toCIDR Render an ip record as a CIDR string. Arguments addr : The ip record to render Example toCIDR (ip 10 42 0 5 16) => "10.42.0.5/16" lib.ipv4.toNetworkAddress Drop the individual octets from an ip record, keeping just address and prefixLength . Arguments addr : The ip record to trim Example toNetworkAddress (ip 10 42 0 5 16) => { address = "10.42.0.5"; prefixLength = 16; } lib.ipv4.toNumber Convert an ip record to its 32-bit integer representation. Arguments addr : The ip record to convert Example toNumber (ip 10 42 0 5 16) => 170524677 lib.ipv4.fromNumber Build an ip record from its 32-bit integer representation and a prefix length. The inverse of toNumber . Arguments addr ( Int ): The 32-bit address prefixLength ( Int ): The CIDR prefix length Example fromNumber 170524677 16 => { a = 10; b = 42; c = 0; d = 5; prefixLength = 16; address = "10.42.0.5"; } lib.ipv4.fromString Parse a CIDR string into an ip record. Arguments str ( String ): A string in "a.b.c.d/prefixLength" form Example fromString "10.42.0.5/16" => { a = 10; b = 42; c = 0; d = 5; prefixLength = 16; address = "10.42.0.5"; } lib.ipv4.fromIPString Parse a bare dotted-decimal string plus a separate prefix length into an ip record. Arguments str ( String ): A string in "a.b.c.d" form, with no prefix length prefixLength ( Int ): The CIDR prefix length Example fromIPString "10.42.0.5" 16 => { a = 10; b = 42; c = 0; d = 5; prefixLength = 16; address = "10.42.0.5"; } lib.ipv4.network Zero out the host bits of an ip record, returning the base address of its subnet. Arguments addr : The ip record to normalize Example toCIDR (network (fromString "10.42.3.7/24")) => "10.42.3.0/24"

docs.text: k8s lib.k8s.createNamespace Build a Kubernetes Namespace manifest for namespace . Arguments namespace ( String ): The namespace's name Example createNamespace { namespace = "media"; } => { apiVersion = "v1"; kind = "Namespace"; metadata.name = "media"; } lib.k8s.replaceInvalidCharacters Replace every character in string that doesn't match validCharsRE with replaceWith . Arguments validCharsRE ( String ): A regular expression matched against each character individually replaceWith ( String ): The replacement for characters that don't match string ( String ): The string to sanitize Example replaceInvalidCharacters "[a-z0-9-]" "-" "My_Path/To.File" => "-y--ath--o--ile" lib.k8s.pathToMountName Turn a filesystem path into a name safe for use as a Kubernetes resource or volume mount name: strips the leading / , lowercases it, and replaces every character outside [a-z0-9-] with - . If the result is longer than 63 characters (the usual Kubernetes name length limit), it's truncated to 54 characters plus a - and an 8-character hash of the full cleaned name, to stay under the limit without losing uniqueness. Arguments path ( String ): The path to convert Example pathToMountName "/data/media/downloads" => "data-media-downloads" lib.k8s.buildKustomization Build a derivation that renders the kustomization at path inside src into a single Kubernetes manifest, via kubectl kustomize . extraFiles are copied in before building -- useful for files the kustomization references that aren't already part of src . If options is given, it's serialized into a ConfigMap named options and written to ${path}/options.yaml , marked with the config.kubernetes.io/local-config annotation so kustomize treats it as local, non-deployed configuration (for use with generators or replacements inside the kustomization). Arguments pkgs : nixpkgs name ( String ): Used only for the derivation's own name src : Derivation or path containing the kustomization entrypoint and any relative bases it references path ( String ): Path inside src to build ( optional , defaults to "." ) options : Value to serialize into the options ConfigMap ( optional ) extraFiles ( { [DestPath] :: SrcPath } ): Additional files to copy in before building ( optional ) Example k8s.buildKustomization { inherit pkgs; } { name = "media"; src = ./kustomize/media; } lib.k8s.patchManifest Build a derivation that applies patch to the single manifest src via kubectl kustomize , and returns the patched manifest. Arguments pkgs : nixpkgs src : The manifest file to patch patch : The kustomize patch file to apply Example k8s.patchManifest { inherit pkgs; } ./deployment.yaml ./patches/replicas.yaml

docs.text: nixos-homelab-storage Databases and persistent storage on top of nixos-homelab : the PostgreSQL and Redis instances that apps in the other repos keep their data in, PersistentVolumes on an NFS export, and Samba file sharing on the host. For the full list of module options, see the options reference . Setup { inputs = { ... homelab-storage = { url = "github:nixos-homelab/storage"; inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs"; }; ... }; } { inputs, ... }: { imports = [ inputs.homelab-storage.nixosModules.postgresql ]; config.homelab.postgresql = { enable = true; databases.myapp.backup.enable = true; }; } Modules postgresql : a shared PostgreSQL instance with declarative database creation and backups. redis : a shared Redis instance with a database-index registry, to keep workloads from colliding on the same DB number. nfs-provisioner : a dynamic PersistentVolume provisioner backed by an NFS export. smb : Samba file sharing, with per-user passwords set up through setup-secrets .
